sections.text:
1 Introduction One of humankind’s
significant challenges to economic growth
is to satisfy the increasing demands of the growing population without
causing any adverse effects on the environment. The primary factors
leading to the degradation of natural environmental conditions are
the ever-increasing population, industrial pollution, vehicle exhaust,
and open waste incineration. To mitigate the degradation of the ecosystem
and ensure a safer and improved habitat for humans, animals, and plants,
it is imperative to monitor these pollutants consistently. Several
issues have risen due to the regular emission of different
chemical pollutants into the environment, including nitrogen oxides
(NO 
 x 
 ), ammonia (NH 3 ), methane
(CH 4 ), sulfur oxides (SO 
 x 
 ),
carbon monoxide (CO), suspended particulate matter, lead aerosol,
volatile organic compounds (VOC), and so on from different sources.
Environmental protection organizations and the government have made
incredible efforts to reduce the effects of pollution on society. 
 Environmental pollution has different facets.
The most significant
aspect is air pollution, while other aspects include water and soil
pollution. Both humans and the ecosystem suffer when hazardous gases
are present in the environment. Any toxic gas has the potential to
quickly spread across a large area, resulting in catastrophic damage.
Due to this, people are significantly more susceptible to infections
that cause damage to the lungs and reduce lung function.  As a result, there is a need for an environmental
pollution monitoring system that is equipped with the tools necessary
to quickly identify and quantify the sources of pollution coming from
harmful substances. To accurately measure the toxic gases, analytical
methods, namely,
gas chromatography (GC), spectrophotometry, and high-performance liquid
chromatography (HPLC), were acclaimed. Although these techniques are
exact and precise, they often have significant disadvantages, such
as expensive costs, nonportability, and high-power requirements. Additionally,
implementing such approaches frequently necessitates intricate and
drawn-out pretreatment procedures and trained machinists. Evidently,
these methods cannot offer real-time information about gas exposure.
So, there is a need for low-cost, portable sensing equipment, which
necessitates using micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) technology
in gas sensing applications. 
 The
research on gas sensors and materials has grown significantly
in the last five decades due to the implementation of stringent environmental
pollution regulations concerning the emission of harmful gases. In
the 1960s, metal oxide films have been used in environmental gas sensor
studies. Thermally evaporated ZnO sensors of thickness 1–100
nm were described by Seiyama et al. in 1962,  for detecting several VOCs, hydrocarbons, and carbon dioxide at
temperatures above 400 °C. The majority of currently available
commercial gas sensors are
developed by using polymer materials and metal oxide semiconductors.
However, these gas sensors may have one or more drawbacks: High power
consumption, poor selectivity, limited lifespan, low repeatability,
expensive, low sensitivity at lower parts per million or parts per
billion levels, and difficulty miniaturizing. Alternatively, nanostructured
material-based gas sensors have grown significantly in relevance due
to several promising electrical, thermal, and optical properties. 
 Electrochemical sensing is the most widely
used approach for monitoring
atmospheric toxic pollutants when compared to methods like optical,  acoustic,  and gas
chromatographic methods.  Strong selectivity
and repeatability, ppm level detection with high accuracy, low energy
linear output with high resolution, and a reduced cost are all significant
advantages of electrochemical detection over other techniques.  These sensors are fabricated with various functional
materials such as carbon nanomaterials, metallic nanostructures, organic
materials, transition metal dichalcogenides, gallium nitride, zeolite,
and others. Compared to nonoptical sensing methods with longer
lifetimes, utilizing
optical methods quickly improves sensitivity, selectivity, and stability.
These sensing methods have short response times. Environmental changes,
catalyst poisoning from particular gases, etc., will not affect its
performance. Smart polymers, metals, metal oxides, and semiconductor
materials have been used to create the sensing layers to improve the
sensitivity and selectivity of the optical sensors effectively. Sensing
materials, including SnO 2 , Sm 2 O 3 ,
Bi 2 O 3 , ZnO, and WO 3 , have been widely
employed because of adjustable physicochemical features, conductivity,
and cost-effectiveness. Due to the resulting interactions, which
may even be seen at low
gas concentration levels, the acoustic sensor offers substantially
more excellent environmental pollutant detection performance. Almost
all acoustic wave sensors produce acoustic waves using a piezoelectric
material. The most popular materials for piezoelectric substrates
that are utilized for acoustic wave sensors and devices are quartz
(SiO 2 ), lithium tantalate (LiTaO 3 ), and, to
a lesser extent, lithium niobate (LiNbO 3 ). In this
paper, different sensing methods and sensing materials
adopted for detecting environmental pollutants are reviewed, focusing
on hazardous gases like nitrogen oxides (NO 
 x 
 ), ammonia (NH 3 ), carbon monoxide (CO), and sulfur
oxides (SO 
 x 
 ). The working principle of
sensing technology adopted for fabricating sensors, sensing materials
used, and important sensing parameters like sensitivity, operating
temperature, and detection range were thoroughly analyzed to detect
environmental pollutants. The paper’s organization is
as follows:  Section 2  discusses the working
principle of four different
sensing technologies: electrochemical, solid state, optical, and acoustic.
Recent research on hazardous gas detection is reviewed in  Section 3 , and  Section 4  concludes.

2 Pollution Monitoring Sensors The most
vulnerable aspect of pollution, air pollution, is caused
by various things, including human activity, industrial operations,
and the expulsion of solid, liquid, and gaseous substances into the
environment. There are two forms of air pollutants, as shown in  Figure  
 . The main air pollutant
is emitted directly into the atmosphere from a source. The source
of the emissions might be either anthropogenic, originating from industrial
and vehicle activities, or natural, arising from events such as sandstorms
and volcanic eruptions. The secondary air pollutant is caused by the
physical interaction between the primary or primary pollutants and
other environmental elements. Many hazardous gases have been identified
in the environment. So, various organizations and agencies worldwide
have developed several clean air quality standards. The air quality
index (AQI) is a benchmark for measuring the degree of air pollution
and providing a quantitative interpretation. The breakpoint of AQI
defined by Indian national air quality standards has six ranking levels
from reasonable to severe. Here, CO is measured in mg/m 3  and other pollutants in μg/m 3 . For CO and O 3 , an hourly mean value is taken; for different pollutants,
two mean values are considered. 1 Sources of air pollutants [Source:  https://energyeducation.ca/ ] Adapted from G. Tyler Miller, Jr. and D. Hackett, “Outdoor
Air Pollution”. In  Living in the Environment , 2nd ed. Nelson: USA, 2011; Chapter 20, section 2, pp 461–465. The usage of automobiles and the consumption of
fossil fuels are
growing significantly due to advancements in technology, which results
in a substantial negative impact on the atmosphere. Sensors must be
developed to detect air pollution sources and maintain the environment’s
standard concentration. In contrast to conventional gas sensors, sensing
methods such as electrochemical, solid state, optical, and acoustic
have several advantages. These include increased sensitivity, reduced
power consumption, smaller designs, and a significantly cheaper cost
of manufacture. 
 − 
 
 
 2.1 Working Principle of Various Sensing Technologies Many advancements in gas sensors have been achieved recently, but
each technology utilized has strengths and limitations of its own.
The most common categories of gas sensors include electrochemical,
solid state, optical, and acoustic. 2.1.1 Electrochemical Sensors Various
analyte compounds are concentrated in tested samples using electrochemical
sensors. Toxic gases, including CO, H 2 , SO 2 ,
and others, are frequently detected by using electrochemical sensors.
Electrochemical sensors detect target analytes by converting chemical
information into an electrical signal through electrochemical reactions.
The core principle involves redox (reduction–oxidation) reactions
that take place at an electrode surface in the presence of an analyte.
The key benefit of the electrochemical sensor compared to other sensors
is its lower power usage. In a typical electrochemical sensor,
a thin electrolytic layer separates the sensing electrode from the
counter electrode, as shown in  Figure  
 a. The working electrode interacts with the target
gas as it diffuses through the selectively permeable barrier, initiating
a specific chemical or electrochemical reaction on its surface. This
reaction leads to a measurable change in the properties of the sensing
material, most commonly its electrical conductivity. The change in
conductivity is directly influenced by the concentration of the target
gas and serves as the primary indicator of its presence. This variation
is then detected and processed by the sensor’s circuitry, which
converts it into a corresponding electrical signal. The resulting
signal is proportional to the gas concentration, allowing for quantitative
analysis and the precise monitoring of the detected substance. Potentiometric,
amperometric, conductometric, and voltametric sensors come under the
category of electrochemical sensors. Potentiometric sensors measure
the potential difference between a working electrode and a reference
electrode at zero current. Amperometric sensors measure the current
generated due to the oxidation or reduction of an analyte at a fixed
potential. Conductometric sensors measure changes in electrical conductivity
due to ion interactions, and voltametric sensors apply a varying voltage
and measure the resulting current to study redox behavior. 2 Schematic view
of an (a) electrochemical sensor, (b) MOS sensor,
and (c) chemiresistive sensor. 2.1.2 Solid State Sensors Chemiresistive
and metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) sensors come under the same category
of solid-state sensors, i.e., providing output based on the resistance
changes. 
 , 
 
 MOS sensors: The first MOS sensor
was developed by means of zinc oxide (ZnO) films to detect CO. Since
then, a lot of research has been carried out in MOS technology to
improve its performance for various applications. The basic design
of MOS consists of a sensing layer (to sense various concentrations
of gases and produce electrical resistance as output), dual interaction
electrodes, substrates, and a warming element among the substrates
as shown in  Figure  
 b. The basic working principle of the MOS sensors depends on the
surface reaction of oxygen molecules. 
 − 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  As an n or p type material is used for the sensing layer, the MOS
sensor exhibits different characteristics for the same target gas.
For the n-type sensing material, the output resistance increases;
for the p-type sensing material, the output resistance decreases for
the oxidizing target gas. Meanwhile, for reducing target gas, the
output resistance decreases for the n-type sensing material and increases
for the p-type sensing material. To improve the sensitivity, the sensing
layer must be heated to 250 °C.  Many
researchers have researched sensing materials to enhance the performance
of the MOS gas sensor’s performance. The commonly used sensing
materials are zinc oxide (ZnO), titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ),
ferric oxide (Fe 3 O 2 ), and tin oxide (SnO 2 ). 
 , 
  SnO 2  is a widely used
sensing material due to its stability. Chemiresistive sensors:
These sensors work on the principle of
change in electrical resistance due to chemical reactions on the exterior
of the sensing component. Chemiresistive sensors do not use microheaters
as used in MOS sensors as shown in  Figure  
 c. The change in resistance depends on the
target gas properties and concentration. Fabricating these sensors
is simple since the basic design consists of two electrodes and a
sensing material. Flexible chemoresistive sensors are also available
using polymer substrates. Recent researchers use nanostructured materials
for the sensing layer. In a study,  a
very sensitive nanostructured dye-doped polypyrrole electrosynthesis
was developed using gold interdigitated electrodes (IDE). The detection
limit for 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene (TNT) was reported to be 0.2 ppb,
while the dynamic range was 9.7–827 ppb. Commonly, the electrodes
are fabricated in an interdigitated structure, which maximizes the
contact area. The major drawback of the chemiresistive sensors is
its sensing layer which is more prone to humidityn thereby affecting
the sensitivity of the sensors. 
 , 
 
 2.1.3 Optical Sensors The sensors that
are commonly used are fiber optic and photonic crystal cavities. Fiber optic sensors: These sensors are suggested for applications
involving ecological monitoring. The sensors are arranged in an array
with a sensing unit having a variable selectivity to distinguish different
analytes. Due to the size of the optical cable, the miniaturization
of fiber-optic sensors may be limited. They are, nevertheless, said
to have good selectivity, sensitivity, and stability. The sensing
layer corresponds to core and clad. During the fabrication process
for sensors, the core and cladding
indexes are removed and replaced with the sensing layer with a high
refractive index on top of the modified clad layer. Target gases will
cause this modified cladding layer’s optical characteristics
to alter, which will affect the sensing layer’s refractive
index as shown in  Figure  
 a. 
 3 Schematic view of (a)
fiber optic sensors and (b) photonic crystal
sensors. Photonic crystal sensors: These sensors utilize
the periodic arrangements
of dielectric material with varying refractive indexes to measure
the refractive index. Similar to the way semiconductor crystals affect
electron motion, these materials have an impact on photon mobility.
The arrangement of the dielectric material within the photonic crystals
results in the photonic bandgap (PBG). Specific frequencies or wavelengths
of light within are forbidden from passing the photonic crystals.
As a result, photonic crystals can modify light transmission and create
properties that are not achievable with traditional optics.  Photonic crystal sensors are used to identify
the target gas in gas sensing applications by measuring the diffraction
wavelength change.  Figure  
 b displays a schematic representation of the photonic crystal
sensor. The two factors that change the diffraction wavelength are
a change in effective refractive index and a modification in lattice
length of periodic structure.  The sensing
principle of photonic crystals can be explained by using Bragg’s
law as given in  eq  
 
 
 m λ = 2 n d sin θ 
 1 
 where  m  refers
to the diffraction order, λ denotes the incident wavelength,  n  refers to the effective refractive index,  d  refers to the lattice spacing, and θ is the incident angle.
Assuming that the incident angle is fixed when the gas particles transit
through the photonic crystals, the effective refractive index  n  and the lattice spacing  d  change, thereby
changing the diffraction wavelength and gaseous detection.  Self-assembly methods like advanced micropatterning
or advanced MEMS fabrication methods like electron beam lithography
or chemical vapor deposition are carried out to construct photonic
crystals from which the crystal dimensions can be controlled. 
 , 
 
 2.1.4 Acoustic Sensors Acoustic sensors
use acoustic waves for the detection of gases. They detect gas molecules
that may be adsorbed on the sensing layer’s surface and react
to the analytes’ absorption in the sensing film. The analytes
with greater chemical interactions can be detected in these sensors
even at lower gas concentrations.  The
limited selectivity is a significant issue in acoustic sensors. The
quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) and surface acoustic wave (SAW)
sensors fall under this category. QCM sensors: When piezoelectric
crystals such as quartz are subjected to mechanical stress, they become
electrically polarized. The atoms in the material will be displaced
when the crystal is deformed. The operating principle of QCM is characterized
by the variation in mass on the surface of the quartz crystal, which
determines its oscillation frequency. These sensors utilize a piezoelectric
quartz crystal, which is positioned among two electrodes and covered
with the substance under sensing, as depicted in  Figure  
 a. The fundamental principle  is given in  eq  
 
 
 Δ f = s f 0 2 ρ q u q Δ m A 
 2 
 where  Δf  is the shift in resonant frequency (Hz),  s  is the
change in mass due to surface adsorption (g),  f 
 0  is the reference resonant frequency (Hz),  A  refers to the active area of QCM on electrodes,  ρ 
 q  is the surface mass density of crystal (g/cm 3 ) and  u 
 q  is the shear modulus of crystal
(Pa). In the gas detection mechanism, the surface molecules in the
sensing layer absorb the target gas, thereby inducing mass variation,
which decreases the resonant frequency. The QCM sensors detect the
mass change due to surface absorption by measuring the shift in the
resonant frequency. The QCM sensor typically generates a frequency
ranging from 5 to 10 MHz, which is based on the depth of quartz crystal. 
 , 
  A thin layer of gas-sensitive material with good adsorption capability
must be applied to the surface of the QCM to enhance its sensitivity.  The advantages of QCM-based acoustic gas sensing
for detecting gaseous pollutants include a more compact device dimension
and enhanced sensitivity. Conversely, QCM gas sensors are characterized
by a reduced signal-to-noise proportion owing to surface interference
in the crystal, a more intricate manufacturing process, and a reduced
sensitivity compared to SAW sensors. 
 4 Schematic
view of (a) QCM sensors and (b) SAW sensors. SAW sensors: These sensors detect the changes in
the environment
through physical properties of surface waves. The fundamental design
of the SAW sensors consists of a substrate made of piezoelectric material
and a pair of SAW reflector arrays detached by a void where a duo
of electrodes or interdigital transducers (IDT) is present. The wave
action subsequently generates surface acoustic waves. When exposed
to foreign substances, this layer’s mass, mechanical
characteristics, or electric properties change, disturbing the surface
waves enabling the use of the devices as sensors. For gas sensing
applications, SAW devices are coated with a layer of suitable material,
including metals, polymers, and metal oxides. 
 , 
  The major drawback while using a polymer as a sensing layer is that
it gets easily affected by the humidity, which creates significant
losses and low propagation velocity. The advantages include high sensitivity,
compact design, and shorter detection time.

4 Conclusions and Future Insights Due
to several factors like pollution, climate change, and disturbances
related to biodiversity, environmental sustainability is a constant
and growing issue. This work investigated the recent research on critical
environmental pollutants regarding sensing materials, sensing technologies,
and sensing performance parameters. Four different gas sensing technologies
(electrochemical, solid state, optical, and acoustic) were studied,
and it is found that metal oxide semiconductor-based sensing technology
is widely used at a large scale for sensing different environmental
pollutants. Substantial developments are achieved in sensitivity,
selectivity, portability, and range of detection for gases like NO 
 x 
 , NH 3 , CO, and SO 
 x 
  by using different sensing materials. However, these
sensors have limitations in essential parameters like operating temperature,
fabrication cost, response, recovery time, etc. Addressing these challenges
will likely involve the development of advanced materials, such as
nanostructured or bioinspired composites, to enhance sensor sensitivity
and robustness. And also, these restrictions can be eliminated by
utilizing proper heterostructures and implementing affordable manufacturing
methods. Self-powered sensors, utilizing energy harvesting mechanisms,
such as piezoelectric, thermoelectric, or photovoltaic systems, are
anticipated to address power limitations and support extended deployment
in remote or inaccessible locations. Advances in miniaturization and
the development of flexible electronics are expected to enable seamless
integration into complex monitoring networks. This study will provide
current and future research with an overview of the current state
of the art for the above-mentioned environmental pollutant sensors.
